prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which made it possible to measure market power and the effects of mergers and policy with real data

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B005 with Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. The chair asks for one test applied to all four leading candidates. Mine has four parts. Did the work change what can be credibly known? Has it been validated by long use and critique? Is the credit attributable to a small set of people? Does it add something distinct from earlier prizes? On the first two, the BLP demand framework does very well. Random-coefficients demand with endogenous prices lets researchers recover substitution patterns, markups and welfare effects from market data. It is used routinely in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and in trade, health and environmental work. The core is a single jointly authored contribution that is about three decades old, so lasting influence can be judged from the record. No colleague has raised a timing or prior-prize overlap problem for B005. That is a real advantage over B014, B027 and B030, where distinctness from the 2024, 2022 and 2023-24 prizes is contested. I regard B014, B027 and B030 as strong candidates, and I have the same doubts about each under the same test. B014 has a coherent programme but weaker identification and an overlap question. B027 has a clean mechanism but indirect validation. B030 has design-based evidence but unsettled persistence and a two-strand credit set. I would not call B005 a clear winner on every dimension. It does best on validation in use together with attribution that can be agreed. On scope, I keep the citation to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets. That is what all three named people share. Pakes's dynamic-industry work is real, but it would overstate the credit of Berry and Levinsohn if the citation claimed it for them.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. This is a methods and measurement prize without one headline finding about the economy, and a committee that weights substantive discoveries more heavily could reasonably rank B030 or B014 higher. The three-name cap excludes Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, and Bresnahan in particular has a strong claim to the earlier tradition of inferring market power. I changed my third name from Bresnahan to Levinsohn because a demand-estimation citation should credit the authors of the paper it rests on. That choice would not hold if the Committee wanted a broader empirical-IO citation. BLP-type estimates are also sensitive to instruments, functional form and implementation. That is a limit on how much applied results can be treated as settled, even if it does not undermine the originality of the method. Finally, I work in industrial organisation, so I may overweight this field. I try to counter that by stating the common test explicitly and by naming the weaknesses of B005 as well as those of the others.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B005 first and words the citation to include dynamic models of industries. He argues that the measurement contribution is itself the discovery, and he accepts Bresnahan instead of Levinsohn if colleagues judge that rewarding the earlier tradition is more faithful to how the field developed.
responses.response: I agree that measurement can be a discovery, and I apply the same test to every candidate. My disagreement is on the citation wording. If the citation includes dynamic industry models, it should name Benkard, Levin and other contributors to that strand, or it will credit Berry and Levinsohn with work that was not theirs. With the cap at three names, I prefer to keep the citation to demand and competition, where Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes share the credit. On Bresnahan we are close. I would also take the broader tradition only as a deliberate change of both citation and credit set, and I note that this would open a different set of attribution disputes.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B014 first and calls the B005 contest close. He would not oppose B005 if the Committee weighs breadth of use more heavily. His main argument is that B014 rewards both a framework and a body of substantive findings, whereas B005 is mainly a toolkit.
responses.response: I accept that B014 is a coherent, mature programme and that the 2024 overlap is arguable either way. My preference does not depend on that overlap. It depends on identification. The constitutional and electoral-rule evidence is mostly cross-country, and you list that among your own reservations. I would want the citation for any B014 award to say clearly which of its results are well identified. On your toolkit-versus-findings point, I think the difference is smaller than it seems. BLP estimates produce substantive findings, such as markups, merger effects and the value of new products, in many markets. I disclose that I have co-authored with you, and I do not treat our agreement on adjacent topics as independent evidence in either direction.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B027 first and weights conceptual originality and durable influence on how macroeconomists think above the number of fields that use a tool. He concedes that the amplification mechanism is validated more indirectly than B005 and that overlap with the 2022 prize is a real question.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a conceptual advance with the cleanest two-person attribution. I also agree that I should not use breadth of use as the only criterion, which is why my test has four parts. Under that test, B027 does best on originality and attribution. It does less well on direct validation and has a stated adjacency to 2022. B005 does best on validation in use and has no stated overlap problem. Our difference is mostly how to weigh validation against originality, which cannot be settled by counting supporters. I would add that the mechanism's influence on central-bank and macro-financial models is also a form of use, so I do not see breadth as an argument that favours only B005. I regard B027 as a credible alternative.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B027 first. He says breadth of use should apply equally to Kiyotaki-Moore, that the diffuse-attribution objection to B005 is smaller once colleagues converge on a Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core, and that Friberg's earlier choice of Bresnahan showed the boundary was contested.
responses.response: That is a fair point about my opening, and it is why I revised the third name. The boundary was contested, but it was contested within a citation that did not yet say what it rewarded. Once the citation is tied to demand estimation with endogenous prices, the three-person core is the natural unit. I accept your point on equal application of the criterion, and I try to apply it as the four-part test above. I also defer to you and others on how much weight indirect empirical validation should carry for a theory contribution of this age. That judgement is not one I can settle from the supplied files.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B030 first. She argues that it combines a framework with newly assembled data and quasi-experimental identification, and that the China-shock design is a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution. She accepts that persistence and magnitude of the effects, and shift-share identification, are still debated.
responses.response: I agree that design-based evidence of this kind is valuable, and I ranked B030 fifth in my opening and keep it as an alternative. On the common test, B030 does very well on changing what can be credibly known. It is weaker on settled validation because persistence is still debated, and it asks the Committee to decide whether the technology and trade strands form one prize or two. I accept your Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio over adding Katz. I would not call B030 less meritorious than B005. I would call it somewhat less settled on maturity, which is the criterion where the two differ most.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a narrow demand-estimation citation or a broader empirical-IO citation that would bring in Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard or Levin. A broader citation would change both the wording and the credit set, and I cannot show that it would be better.
How to weigh a methods and measurement contribution against substantive findings such as B014 or B030. Members have not agreed on one test, and mine is one judgement among several.
How far sensitivity of BLP-type estimates to implementation, instruments and functional form should qualify the claim that the framework is a settled body of knowledge.

I have not verified claims about prior prizes, replication records, citation counts or the identification quality of other candidates. They rest on colleagues' statements in the files and my own general knowledge.
Whether B025 should rank higher as an alternative once the credit of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum relative to Melitz and Helpman is settled. Colleagues' round 1 statements leave this unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: I disclose that my research is in industrial organisation and pricing, which is field proximity to B005, and I may favour it, so I rely on a stated common test. The profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn, or to any other credited name on the shortlist. I have co-authored with committee colleagues John Hassler (chair, who prefers B014) and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). My co-authors Chad Syverson, Itay Goldstein and the others listed in my profile do not appear among the credited names. These ties bear on committee relationships, not on a candidate, and I do not adjudicate them. I am married to a former Swedish prime minister, which is a public fact with no apparent bearing on this ballot. My disagreement with Hassler on B014 should not be read as an independent signal either way.
